intro: Saudi culture is rooted in Islam, Bedouin desert traditions and generous hospitality. In recent years it has opened up to concerts, cinema and tourism.

chapters.title: Coffee, dates and kabsa
text: Guests are welcomed with Arabic coffee, flavoured with cardamom and poured into small cups, and dates. Refusing is impolite; giving the cup a little shake means you've had enough.
The national dish is kabsa, spiced rice cooked with chicken or lamb, often eaten from a large shared platter.

chapters.title: Desert traditions
text: Falconry, training birds of prey to hunt, is a prized tradition. Camels are central to Bedouin life, and there are camel races, now ridden by small robot jockeys, and even camel beauty contests.
Al-Ardah, a sword dance with drums and poetry, is performed at national celebrations and is on UNESCO's heritage list. Poetry, especially in the Bedouin style called Nabati, is highly respected.

chapters.title: Heritage and new arts
text: Historic sites include the coral-stone houses of old Jeddah, the mud-brick palaces of At-Turaif in Diriyah and the tombs of Hegra. Cinemas were banned for 35 years until 2018; Wadjda (2012), the first feature film shot entirely in Saudi Arabia, was directed by a woman, Haifaa al-Mansour.
Entertainment festivals such as Riyadh Season now bring concerts, theme parks and sports events to the capital.

keyTerms.meaning: Arab peoples who traditionally lived as desert nomads, herding camels and goats.
Hunting with trained falcons or other birds of prey.
